recent_posts.title: UTF-8, Explained Simply
recent_posts.summary: UTF-8 is a variable-width character encoding system that has become the dominant standard for text on the web. It achieves backward compatibility with ASCII by using the unused eighth bit to indicate multi-byte sequences, while maintaining self-synchronization through clever bit patterns that distinguish leading bytes from continuation bytes. The encoding can represent over 2 million code points using 1-4 bytes, with the number of leading ones in the first byte indicating the total length. This design allows UTF-8 to efficiently encode ASCII text in single bytes while supporting all Unicode characters, making it both space-efficient and universally compatible.

The course applies the zone of proximal development theory, building concepts step-by-step to avoid knowledge gaps. It covers machine code, how programming languages work, and low-level concepts, available through Patreon for $8/month with additional perks like Discord access and early video releases.

recent_posts.title: Recursion, Explained Simply
recent_posts.summary: Recursion is a programming concept where functions call themselves, but it can be challenging to understand and has practical limitations like stack overflow errors. The explanation covers how recursive functions work under the hood using the call stack, demonstrates file system traversal as a practical example, and shows how to convert recursive functions to iterative ones using manual stack management. It explores different traversal patterns (depth-first vs post-order) and addresses real-world concerns like memory limitations and infinite loops.

recent_posts.title: Data Structures, Explained Simply
recent_posts.summary: Computer memory functions as a large array of sequential boxes with addresses, and all data structures are built on top of this fundamental concept. The article explains how different arrangements of data in arrays create various data structures like sorted arrays, array lists, stacks, queues, linked lists, hashmaps, trees, and graphs. Each structure offers different trade-offs in performance for operations like searching, inserting, and deleting elements. Key concepts include how stacks and queues restrict access to specific ends, how linked lists use pointers to maintain order without relying on array positioning, how hashmaps use hash functions to convert keys into array indices, and how trees and graphs represent hierarchical and networked relationships respectively.

recent_posts.title: HashMaps & Dictionaries, Explained Simply
recent_posts.summary: Hash maps (dictionaries) solve the problem of efficiently finding data using keys instead of numeric indexes. They work by using hash functions to convert keys into array indexes, but face challenges like collisions when different keys produce the same hash. Two main approaches handle collisions: open addressing (linear probing through a single array) and closed addressing (using linked lists in separate arrays). Open addressing offers better lookup performance but suffers from clustering and complex resizing, while closed addressing provides easier deletion and resizing but with slower random access performance.

recent_posts.title: Allocators, Explained Simply
recent_posts.summary: Memory allocators work like government budget distribution, taking limited resources and dividing them among different programs. Linear allocators are the simplest type, tracking memory with a single address pointer, but they create fragmentation when programs exit out of order. Modern operating systems solve this by dividing memory into small blocks that can be reused, allowing non-contiguous allocation. Linear allocators remain valuable for stack-based operations where memory is always freed in reverse order, making them perfect for function call management where stack frames are allocated and deallocated following the natural execution flow.

recent_posts.title: Memory Arenas, Explained Simply
recent_posts.summary: Memory arenas are a simple memory management technique where you allocate one large chunk of memory upfront and place multiple smaller objects inside it. Instead of deallocating each object individually, you deallocate the entire arena at once, eliminating memory leaks and improving performance. This concept is already familiar to programmers through stack frames in function calls, and can be applied to scenarios like HTTP request processing where related data has the same lifecycle.

recent_posts.title: The real technical cause behind the Y2K bug and BCD mode
recent_posts.summary: The Y2K bug wasn't simply about using two digits to save space, but specifically about how older computer systems used Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) mode to store dates. Unlike regular binary representation, BCD stores each decimal digit separately as a 4-bit binary number, making conversion between human-readable decimal and machine-readable binary more efficient on older hardware. This explains why dates would overflow from 99 to 00, as each decimal digit was stored individually rather than as a single binary number. The technical explanation reveals why the common oversimplified narrative about memory constraints misses the crucial detail about how numbers were actually represented in legacy systems.

recent_posts.title: Mathematical notation is designed for professionals, not learners
recent_posts.summary: Mathematical notation is intentionally designed to be correct, unambiguous, and compact for professional use, but these same properties make it inherently difficult to learn. The compactness leads to information hiding where symbols and operations are omitted, creating confusing exceptions and rules that students must memorize. Examples include how basic arithmetic operations like addition and subtraction become complex when negative numbers are introduced, how the division symbol creates ambiguity, and how the order of operations requires extensive memorization. The author argues that much of math education difficulty stems from notation design rather than the mathematical concepts themselves, suggesting that alternative notations could make learning more intuitive.

recent_posts.title: Intro to Data Oriented Design for Games
recent_posts.summary: Data-oriented design (DOD) offers game developers a systematic approach to CPU performance optimization by focusing on memory layout and cache efficiency. The approach emphasizes processing data in bulk rather than individual objects, using techniques like struct alignment, avoiding pointer indirection, and organizing data by usage patterns. Key principles include minimizing cache misses, processing similar data together, and eliminating branching logic within tight loops. Practical optimizations demonstrated include converting classes to structs, removing function callbacks, hoisting loop invariants, and using specialized data structures like swap-back arrays for efficient deletions.
